metadata.file_name: IEA Compass 14 Coherence between Swedish grades and TIMSS 2015 - June 2021.pdf
metadata.title: Coherence between Swedish grades and TIMSS 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study merges Swedish TIMSS 2015 (grade 8) student test scores with Swedish register data on students’ year-9 final grades and year-9 national test grades, using personal identity numbers collected during TIMSS 2015. The analysis focuses on mathematics and science, recoding the A–F grade scales into numeric values and, for science, weighting final grades across biology, physics, and chemistry to create a single science grade. The manuscript does not report the use of TIMSS sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it does report uncertainty via 95% confidence intervals for mean TIMSS scores, indicating that sampling variability was considered. No explicit complex-survey weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is provided, so it is unclear whether population-representative weighting was applied; the reported coherence is therefore best interpreted as descriptive/associational evidence based on the merged analytic sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This report does not model cognitive achievement using TIMSS plausible values (PVs). Instead, it analyzes coherence between TIMSS test scores and Swedish grade indicators (A–F recoded numerically) and reports correlations and linear regression coefficients with TIMSS scores as outcomes. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores and the paper does not describe any missing-data procedure for the merged dataset, the missing-data handling strategy is not documented; this is a reporting gap for transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Swedish students who participated in TIMSS 2015 (year 8) and for whom personal identity numbers enabled merging with register data containing year-9 final grades in mathematics and science and year-9 national test grades in mathematics and science. The analysis focuses on mathematics and science; for science, final grades across biology, physics, and chemistry were weighted to form a single science grade, and corresponding national test grades were similarly combined. The manuscript does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing covariates, grade-level restrictions, or complete-case rules) beyond the merged availability of the relevant records.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA Compass report validates coherence between Swedish year-9 grades and TIMSS 2015 (year-8) test scores using merged TIMSS and register data for Sweden. Descriptively, TIMSS score distributions shift upward across final grade levels A–F, with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for mean TIMSS scores across grade levels. Correlations are moderately strong: final grades correlate with TIMSS mathematics at r=0.76 and with TIMSS science at r=0.64, while national test grades correlate at about r=0.65 (math) and r=0.62 (science). In linear regression, final grades alone explain 57% of TIMSS mathematics variance and 39% of TIMSS science variance; adding student background (gender, migration background, home resources) increases explained variance to 61% (math) and 49% (science). The manuscript does not report any ML modeling, PV handling, or a missing-data strategy, and it does not clearly document whether TIMSS complex-survey weights were applied.
